- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.27) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive pessimism.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope afterward.  
- If sentiment is high (≥0.80) and price is trending up, model frequently overestimates near-term upside; cap forecast growth at 3–5% above recent high.  
- When sentiment is mixed (0.27–0.53) and price is volatile, model tends to lag behind true trend; shift forecast 1–2 days ahead to align with sentiment momentum.  
- In low-sentiment, low-price environments, model often underestimates downside risk; add 1–2% buffer below forecast to account for mean reversion or policy shocks.  
- If true outcome is significantly below forecast (e.g., >10% gap), check if sentiment was high recently — if so, model may have overestimated bullish sentiment; reduce forecast by 5–10% for next period.
